True Statement: The immense variety of living organisms on Earth is known as biodiversity; every organism plays a role in keeping nature stable and functioning.
False 1: Biodiversity refers only to the variety of animals, not plants or microorganisms.

True Statement: Microscopic algae in the oceans release most of the oxygen we breathe.
False 1: Microscopic algae in the oceans release most of the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
False 2: Cyanobacteria on land release most of the oxygen we breathe.

True Statement: Fungi and bacteria decompose fallen leaves and convert waste into manure, making the soil fertile.
False 1: Algae and plants decompose fallen leaves and convert waste into manure, making the soil fertile.
False 2: Fungi and bacteria synthesise food from sunlight, making the soil fertile.

True Statement: Species restricted to particular regions of the world and not found naturally anywhere else are called endemic species.
False 1: Species found in all regions of the world are called endemic species.
False 2: Species that have undergone significant habitat loss are called endemic species.

True Statement: Regions that support a large number of endemic species and have undergone significant habitat loss are known as biodiversity hotspots.
False 1: Regions that support a large number of endemic species but show no habitat loss are known as biodiversity hotspots.
False 2: Regions that support a large number of exotic (non-native) species are known as biodiversity hotspots.

True Statement: The Western Ghats, Indo-Burma (including North East India), the Himalayas, and Sundaland (including the Nicobar Islands) are examples of global biodiversity hotspots.
False 1: The Deccan Plateau, the Thar Desert, the Eastern Ghats, and the Indo-Gangetic Plain are examples of global biodiversity hotspots.

True Statement: Aristotle, around the 4th century BCE, grouped animals based on their habitat (land, water and air) and external appearances.
False 1: Carolus Linnaeus, around the 4th century BCE, grouped animals based on their habitat (land, water and air).
False 2: Aristotle grouped animals based on their internal anatomy and genetic similarity.

True Statement: In the two kingdom system (18th century), all living organisms were divided into Plantae (synthesise own food, do not move) and Animalia (move and depend on other organisms for food).
False 1: In the two kingdom system, all living organisms were divided into Monera and Eukaryota.
False 2: In the two kingdom system, Plantae includes organisms that move and depend on other organisms for food.

True Statement: Protista was added as a third kingdom to include unicellular microscopic organisms like Amoeba and Paramecium that did not fit Plantae or Animalia.
False 1: Monera was added as a third kingdom to include unicellular microscopic organisms like Amoeba and Paramecium.
False 2: Fungi was added as a third kingdom to include unicellular microscopic organisms.

True Statement: Amoeba has a true (membrane-bound) nucleus but bacteria do not; this difference led bacteria to be placed in a separate kingdom called Monera.
False 1: Bacteria have a true nucleus (membrane-bound) but amoeba does not; this led amoeba to be placed in a separate kingdom called Monera.

True Statement: The kingdom Protista includes mostly unicellular organisms with a true nucleus.
False 1: The kingdom Monera includes mostly unicellular organisms with a true nucleus.

True Statement: Fungi have a heterotrophic mode of nutrition and obtain nutrients by absorption (many absorb from dead and decaying matter); they are placed in a separate kingdom.
False 1: Fungi have an autotrophic mode of nutrition and synthesise food from sunlight.
False 2: Fungi obtain nutrients by ingestion (swallowing food), not by absorption.

True Statement: The five kingdom classification includes Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
False 1: The five kingdom classification includes Monera, Protista, Lichens, Plantae and Animalia.
False 2: The five kingdom classification includes Prokaryota, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

True Statement: Bacteria and cyanobacteria are single-celled prokaryotes grouped under Monera; bacteria are found everywhere, including soil, water, air, hot springs, and inside human bodies.
False 1: Bacteria and cyanobacteria are single-celled eukaryotes grouped under Monera.
False 2: Bacteria and cyanobacteria are grouped under Protista.

True Statement: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) were among the first organisms to produce oxygen through photosynthesis; about 2.5 billion years ago, oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere, making Earth suitable for other forms of life.
False 1: Cyanobacteria were among the first organisms to produce carbon dioxide through respiration.
False 2: About 2.5 million years ago, oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere due to photosynthesis by cyanobacteria.

True Statement: All single-celled eukaryotes without a cell wall or with a cell wall made up of cellulose are grouped under Kingdom Protista; some are autotrophic and others are heterotrophic.
False 1: All single-celled prokaryotes without a cell wall are grouped under Kingdom Protista.
False 2: All single-celled eukaryotes are grouped under Kingdom Monera.

True Statement: Fungi are mostly multicellular eukaryotes with cell walls made of chitin; they do not make their own food; most fungi are saprophytes and play an important ecological role as decomposers.
False 1: Fungi are mostly multicellular eukaryotes with cell walls made of cellulose.
False 2: Fungi are autotrophs that make their own food through photosynthesis.

True Statement: Yeast is a unicellular organism; since its cell wall is made up of chitin, it has been placed under Fungi.
False 1: Yeast is a multicellular organism grouped under Protista.
False 2: Yeast cell wall is made up of cellulose, so it has been placed under Plantae.

True Statement: Plants are multicellular, autotrophic organisms that perform photosynthesis; their cells have a rigid cell wall primarily made up of cellulose; they form the base of most food chains and release oxygen.
False 1: Fungi are multicellular, autotrophic organisms that perform photosynthesis; their cells have a rigid cell wall made up of chitin.
False 2: Animals are multicellular, autotrophic organisms that perform photosynthesis; their cells have a rigid cell wall made up of cellulose.

True Statement: Kingdom Plantae is divided into five classes: Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperm and Angiosperm.
False 1: Kingdom Plantae is divided into four classes: Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Gymnosperm only.
False 2: Kingdom Animalia is divided into five classes: Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperm and Angiosperm.

True Statement: Thallophytes form a simple body called a thallus; they are mostly found in water or moist environments; an example is Spirogyra.
False 1: Bryophytes form a thallus and are mostly found in water or moist environments; an example is Spirogyra.
False 2: Thallophytes possess true roots, stems and leaves and are found in water or moist environments.

True Statement: Bryophytes (mosses and liverworts) have root-like structures called rhizoids and stem-like and leaf-like simple structures; they lack vascular tissues; they require water for reproduction and are called the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'.
False 1: Pteridophytes (ferns) lack vascular tissues and are called the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'.
False 2: Bryophytes possess true roots, stems and leaves with well-developed vascular tissues.

True Statement: Pteridophytes (ferns) possess true roots, stems and leaves; they have vascular tissues (xylem and phloem) that transport water and food; they still depend on water for reproduction and do not produce seeds.
False 1: Bryophytes possess true roots, stems and leaves and have well-developed vascular tissues.
False 2: Pteridophytes produce seeds and do not require water for reproduction.

True Statement: Gymnosperms (e.g., pines, cycads) produce seeds that protect the developing embryo and contain stored food; they do not require aquatic conditions for fertilisation; their seeds are not enclosed in fruits.
False 1: Pteridophytes (ferns) produce seeds and do not require aquatic conditions for fertilisation.
False 2: Gymnosperms produce seeds enclosed within fruits.

True Statement: Angiosperms (flowering plants) produce flowers and fruits; flowers attract pollinators increasing the efficiency of reproduction; fruits help spread seeds to new locations; they are the most diverse plant group on Earth.
False 1: Gymnosperms produce flowers and fruits; flowers attract pollinators; fruits help spread seeds to new locations.
False 2: Angiosperms are the least diverse plant group on Earth because their reproduction is dependent on external pollination agents.

True Statement: Animals are classified into two groups based on the presence or absence of a notochord (a flexible rod-shaped structure): non-chordata (invertebrata) and chordata.
False 1: Animals are classified into non-chordata and chordata based on the presence or absence of a vertebral column (backbone).
False 2: Plants are classified into two groups based on the presence or absence of a notochord: non-chordata and chordata.

True Statement: Sponges (Porifera) are multicellular but lack organisation of tissues and organs; numerous pores allow water to flow through, bringing food particles and oxygen; sponges remain fixed in one place in aquatic environments.
False 1: Sponges (Porifera) are multicellular and have well-organised tissues and organs.
False 2: Hydra (Cnidaria) is multicellular but lacks organisation of tissues and organs and remains fixed in one place.

True Statement: Cnidarians (e.g., Hydra, jellyfish, corals) have tissue-level organisation; they capture prey using tentacles; they possess a single opening that functions for both food intake and waste removal.
False 1: Flatworms (Platyhelminthes) use tentacles for capturing prey and have tissue-level organisation.
False 2: Cnidarians possess two distinct openings — one for food intake and one for waste removal.

True Statement: Flatworms (Platyhelminthes) have bilateral symmetry; their flattened bodies permit efficient diffusion of gases without specialised respiratory organs; they have a single opening for food intake and waste elimination.
False 1: Roundworms (Nematoda) have a single opening for food intake and waste elimination, and bilateral symmetry.
False 2: Flatworms have radial symmetry (body can be divided equally along multiple planes through the centre).

True Statement: Roundworms (Nematoda) have elongated, cylindrical bodies; their body has two openings (mouth and anus).
False 1: Flatworms (Platyhelminthes) have elongated cylindrical bodies with two openings (mouth and anus).
False 2: Roundworms have a flattened body with a single opening for food intake and waste elimination.

True Statement: Arthropods (insects, crabs, spiders) have a hard external skeleton that provides protection, reduces water loss and supports powerful muscles.
False 1: Echinoderms (starfish, sea urchins) have a hard external skeleton that provides protection and reduces water loss.
False 2: Arthropods have a hard internal skeleton that provides protection and support.

True Statement: Echinoderms (starfish, sea urchins) possess a hard internal skeleton made of calcium carbonate; they lack a notochord.
False 1: Arthropods (insects, crabs) possess a hard internal skeleton made of calcium carbonate.
False 2: Echinoderms possess a hard external skeleton made of chitin.

True Statement: Vertebrates possess a vertebral column (backbone), an internal skeletal structure that supports the body and protects vital organs such as the brain and spinal cord.
False 1: Protochordates possess a vertebral column that supports the body and protects vital organs.
False 2: Vertebrates possess a notochord as their permanent internal skeletal structure throughout life.

True Statement: Vertebrates are classified into five groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
False 1: Vertebrates are classified into four groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles and birds only.

True Statement: Binomial nomenclature is a universal system of naming living organisms introduced by Carolus Linnaeus in the 18th century; every organism has a scientific name with two parts (genus and species) written in Latin or a Latinised form.
False 1: Binomial nomenclature was introduced by Aristotle in the 4th century BCE.
False 2: Binomial nomenclature gives every organism a scientific name with three parts (genus, species, and family).

True Statement: In binomial nomenclature: the genus name begins with a capital letter and comes first; the species name is written in small letters; the scientific name is written in italics when printed or underlined when handwritten.
False 1: In binomial nomenclature, the species name begins with a capital letter and comes first; the genus name is written in small letters.
False 2: The scientific name is written in bold when printed and in brackets when handwritten.

True Statement: A genus groups closely related species that share common features; the species name indicates a group of similar organisms capable of interbreeding and producing offspring.
False 1: A species groups closely related genera; the genus name indicates a group of organisms capable of interbreeding.

True Statement: Fossils are preserved remains of plants and animals found in layers of rocks, sand and mud; generally, older layers contain simpler organisms while newer layers show more complex forms.
False 1: Fossils are preserved remains of plants and animals; older layers generally contain more complex organisms while newer layers show simpler forms.

True Statement: Based on genetic data, Carl Woese (1977) proposed the three domain system: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya.
False 1: Based on genetic data, Carolus Linnaeus proposed the three domain system.
False 2: Carl Woese proposed the three domain system: Monera, Protista, and Eukarya.
